en: The boy came raging and distraught.
'Temir Khan and Ismayyl
Have hidden my lineage,' he said,
Taking the deepest offense.
Akshumkar in his hand,
He sent flying toward a plane tree.
The fine white-cloth coat he wore,
He stripped off and flung upon the ground.
The boy would not relent, but raised a quarrel.
He let Aktulpar loose,
Pillowed his head upon the broad-pommeled saddle,
And lay with his head toward the qibla.
Temir Khan's Zulpukor
He laid beside his hip.
From his fierce father Manas,
The fine white-cloth coat worn as a gift,
He spread across himself from head to foot.
He did not open his closed eyes,
Did not draw back his outstretched legs,
Did not stir awake with a groan,
Did not turn to either side,
Made no movement, not the slightest,
The orphan did not move or twitch.
Persisting in protest, distraught,
He had come to the gray mound
And lay there offended.
Temir Khan, khan of Bukhara—
Before Temir Khan
Many people went to bring the news.
Hearing the messenger's words,
'This orphan born of a bloodshedder
Lies there offended,' he heard.
Hearing the words of those who came,
'If he rages in boundless resentment,
This great Bukhara standing here,
He will burn it down,' he heard.
His heart was sorely troubled,
Temir Khan, khan of Bukhara.
Tears poured from his eyes;
His thoughts wandered far away.
Although he had not fathered Semetey,
He had taken him for his son.
His plump little gray-mottled falcon,
He loved him above all mortals,
That Semetey there,
His gray hawk, his morning star.
The spring of his flowing river,
His child gained after long suffering—
Temir Khan hurried in haste
To the mound where Semetey lay.
Coming up, he looked:
Pillowed on the broad-pommeled saddle,
His head turned toward the qibla,
There lay Semetey.
When he saw Semetey,
He prepared an offering to Baabedin.
Seven black bulls
He had driven out through his gate.
Displaying his ample means,
There where the bulls arrived,
He had them slaughtered and cut up.
Doing all manner of things in the open,
As every thought came to mind,
Sixty calves and forty goat wethers
He slaughtered again as an offering.
The wayward boy did not relent.
Then the boy Semetey,
The hapless boy, did not stir.
Truly created by God—
Did you see that he was His servant?
Of poor Manas, the mighty khan,
Did you see that he was his son?
Putting his belt around his neck,
Temir Khan stood wailing,
Pleading with the boy like this:
“My morning star beside the moon,
Oh, Semetey, come this way,
My morning star whom I cherished!
My deep-rooted poplar, my plane tree,
Without seeing you my longing is not quenched.
Rise up, Semetey,
My orphan granted in my last extremity!
My bright star in the sky,
My jewel, my beaver fur upon my collar.
Flowing bright from the valley,
My spring that quenches thirst.
Your father in his old age,
Do not put him alive in the grave.
Rise up, my light!
In this Bukhara,
With my khanly power fully upon me,
I first saw you, my foal,
At sixty-seven years of age.
For whom did I amass gold?
For you, my joy, my child.
Hear my blessing now.
With my beard grown white,
With my journey nearing its end,
Do not cast your father into hell.
Do not burn me with your sulking,
Bringing hardship upon this head.
My foal, do not put me alive in the grave.
Do not burn me like this!
Your horse racing against other horses,
Were you disappointed in your horse?
Your bird flying against other birds,
Were you disappointed in your bird?
Wearing your robe among other robes,
Were you disappointed in this?
Tell me of your sword, tell me of your sheath.
Do not torment me; tell me the truth.
Seven houses full of treasure—
That is the wealth I gathered for you.
Let me axe their entrances open,
Let me spend and scatter it.
A thousand winged steeds in the stable,
A hundred falcons kept in molt,
Giving them away without leaving one,
Let me scatter them in every direction.
Spending my livestock,
My foal, for you, tormenting my own soul,
The four corners of the world,
Sending searchers around them four times,
Let me find the swiftest horse.
The five corners of Medina,
Traveling around them five times,
Let me find the finest hunting bird.
To all the wide world,
Let me send word and say, ‘Hurry!’
Giving a stern command,
Let me seek a robe no shot can pierce.”
Speaking thus, Temir Khan
Now pleaded at length.
To the fierce orphan boy,
He offered many pleas.
Not drawing in his outstretched legs at all,
Not opening his closed eyes at all,
The outstanding child born of Manas,
God had struck the boy.
In haste and alarm, Temir Khan
Saw a disastrous, grievous ordeal.
From this boy he saw danger,
Such a grievous, overwhelming trial.
Seeing this, Temir Khan
Did not stand idly watching.
The learned mullah,
The khoja in a white turban,
The medicine that might bring relief,
Gathering all the people,
The learned mullahs
Read prayers insistently over him.
The boy did not respond to this.
The khojas in motley robes
Recited many prayers.
He did not move a whit.
The wretched orphan did not respond.
His own father Ismayyl,
He too came and pleaded.
That boy Semetey
Was especially resentful toward him.
His grandmother Altynay,
Ismayyl's Kumushay,
Pleaded again and again.
He was especially resentful toward them.
Ismayyl's Kishimjan—
She was a skilled woman,
She was Ismayyl's daughter.
When Kanykey came on her journey to Bukhara,
When she handed over Semetey,
At his nursing-infant age,
She carried him about and raised him,
She was particularly close to him from the start.
Semetey, lord of Bukhara,
That daughter of yours who came,
Was the elder sister Semetey loved as his own life.
Walking up, weeping in distress,
Where she saw the boy,
Pleading as no other mortal did:
“One who would not tire if ridden six months,
My dear Semetey—
My black winged steed, my swift horse,
Moreover, my sibling of the same nest,
My kin, born of the same seed.
My black-blazed hawk,
The one I open my mouth to kiss,
The one I open my eyes to see,
My protecting presence behind me.
Oh, Semetey, my sibling,
Great khan of the fortified city,
Is it right to lie here all day?
Is it fitting for a khan to sulk?
What is this, younger brother, what is this?” she said.
A fattened lamb, sliced horse-neck fat,
Bringing food prepared,
Red raisins and dried grapes,
Liquor and food served with honor,
The lively, impetuous, dauntless woman,
With all kinds of riches mingled,
Heaping sugar like snow,
Filling her tablecloth,
Pressing the boy with pleas,
Calling him ‘sibling,’ she reached out.
The troublesome bitch prepared herself.
“The very image of a king—
My dear sibling,
Is it right to lie like a child?
Father of the people,
Collar of the armored robe,
The shooting bone among many knucklebones,
The winged steed among beasts,
The falcon among winged creatures,
The lion among the fanged,
My honored younger brother Semetey,
Is it right for him to sulk?
Food is a sweet meal—
Can a person take offense at it?
Rise, younger brother, rise,” she said.
“Rise and eat,” she said.
“Do not stay offended so long,” she said.
“I have come making bold.
May I take your troubles upon myself.
Do not lift me up and cast me into misery,” she said.
That bitch who had grown up his companion
Put her arm around his neck,
The orphan touched by Kydyr,
She began to tickle him.
The boy began to rage.
His elder sister doing this,
The outstanding hero's offspring,
As though he would swallow them whole.
His anger came and would not stop,
Without speaking foully or swearing:
“You are misfortune itself!
You have no firmly braced waist,
No place where you have girded yourself,
Led in a string of six gelded camels,
You have no camel that came for hire.
You shameless bitch,
You have no bridegroom to take you.
You have no waist to gird,
No husband to marry.
You have no grounds for mockery.
If you look and make sport,
You have no bridegroom who has come to take you.”
Speaking thus, Semetey,
The wretched orphan who sat glowering,
His elder sister Kishimjan,
Struck her squarely on the cheek.
Not wishing to kiss the bitch,
He shoved her hard away!
Sixty buttons, forty coral beads,
Struck hard by the wrestler's hand,
Shattered into fragments.
Kishimjan, light as a feather,
Went flying with a clatter.
Her precious life hard pressed,
